module_name: Entry into Politics and the Rise of the Nazi Party

extracted_notes.text: In July 1919, he was appointed Verbindungsmann (intelligence agent) of an Aufklarungskommando (reconnaissance unit) of the Reichswehr, assigned to influence other soldiers and to infiltrate the German Workers' Party (DAP).
At a DAP meeting on 12 September 1919, Party chairman Anton Drexler was impressed by Hitler's oratorical skills.
He gave him a copy of his pamphlet My Political Awakening, which contained antisemitic, nationalist, anti-capitalist, and anti-Marxist ideas.

On the orders of his army superiors, Hitler applied to join the party, and within a week was accepted as party member 555 (the party began counting membership at 500 to give the impression they were a much larger party).

Hitler made his earliest known written statement about the Jewish question in a 16 September 1919 letter to Adolf Gemlich (now known as the Gemlich letter). In the letter, Hitler argues that the aim of the government "must unshakably be the removal of the Jews altogether".

At the DAP, Hitler met Dietrich Eckart, one of the party's founders and a member of the occult Thule Society. Eckart became Hitler's mentor, exchanging ideas with him and introducing him to a wide range of Munich society.
To increase its appeal, the DAP changed its name to the Nationalsozialistische Deutsche Arbeiterpartei (National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP), now known as the "Nazi Party").
Hitler designed the party's banner of a swastika in a white circle on a red background.

Friedrich Reck-Malleczewen commented in his 1947 book Diary of a Man in Despair:

 He had come to a house where he had never been before, wearing gaiters, a floppy, wide-brimmed hat, and carrying a riding whip. ... Eventually, he managed to launch into a speech. He talked on and on, endlessly. He preached. He went on at us like a division chaplain in the Army. We did not in the least contradict him, or venture to differ in any way, but he began to bellow at us. The servants thought we were being attacked and rushed in to defend us. When he had gone, we sat silently, confused and not at all amused. There was a feeling of dismay, as when on a train you suddenly find you are sharing a compartment with a psychotic.
In February 1921, already highly effective at crowd manipulation, Hitler spoke to a crowd of over 6,000.

In June 1921, while Hitler and Eckart were on a fundraising trip to Berlin, a mutiny broke out within the Nazi Party in Munich. Members of its executive committee wanted to merge with the Nuremberg-based German Socialist Party (DSP).

Hitler returned to Munich on 11 July and angrily tendered his resignation. The committee members realised that the resignation of their leading public figure and speaker would mean the end of the party. Hitler announced he would rejoin on the condition that he would replace Drexler as party chairman, and that the party headquarters would remain in Munich.
Opponents of Hitler in the leadership had Hermann Esser expelled from the party, and they printed 3,000 copies of a pamphlet attacking Hitler as a traitor to the party.

In the following days, Hitler spoke to several large audiences and defended himself and Esser, to thunderous applause. His strategy proved successful, and at a special party congress on 29 July, he was granted absolute power as party chairman, succeeding Drexler, by a vote of 533 to 1.
Early followers included Rudolf Hess, the former air force ace Hermann Goring, and the army captain Ernst Rohm.
Rohm became head of the Nazis' paramilitary organisation, the Sturmabteilung (SA, "Stormtroopers"), which protected meetings and attacked political opponents.

A critical influence on Hitler's thinking during this period was the Aufbau Vereinigung, a conspiratorial group of White Russian exiles and early Nazis. The group, financed with funds channelled from wealthy industrialists, introduced Hitler to the idea of a Jewish conspiracy, linking international finance with Bolshevism.

The programme of the Nazi Party was laid out in their 25-point programme on 24 February 1920. This did not represent a coherent ideology, but was a conglomeration of received ideas which had currency in the volkisch pan-Germanic movement, such as ultranationalism, opposition to the Treaty of Versailles, distrust of capitalism, as well as some socialist ideas.

blocks.text_content: Following the First World War, Adolf Hitler remained in the German army, but his role shifted from the front lines to the shadows of intelligence. In July 1919, he was tasked with a mission to infiltrate and influence a small political group known as the **German Workers' Party (DAP)**. To do this, he operated under specific military designations that defined his role in the early Weimar Republic.

jargon_buster_data.definition: A reconnaissance unit of the Reichswehr.
An intelligence agent appointed in July 1919 to influence soldiers and infiltrate the German Workers' Party.

blocks.text_content: This assignment placed Hitler in the path of the DAP, where his natural talent for public speaking would soon catch the attention of the party's leadership.

cards.parent_topic: Entry into Politics and the Rise of the Nazi Party

blocks.text_content: On September 12, 1919, Hitler attended a DAP meeting where the party chairman, **Anton Drexler**, was immediately struck by his oratorical power. Drexler introduced Hitler to a pamphlet titled *My Political Awakening*, which laid the groundwork for the antisemitic and nationalist views Hitler would later champion.

itemized_breakdown_data.context_text: Anton Drexler's pamphlet 'My Political Awakening' introduced Adolf Hitler to several key ideological pillars that would shape his early political trajectory.

blocks.text_content: Hitler's entry into the party was marked by a calculated effort to project strength. The DAP used a specific numbering system to make their small group appear more established than it actually was.

blocks.text_content: On September 16, 1919, Hitler wrote a letter to **Adolf Gemlich**. This document is historically significant as it contains the earliest known written statement regarding his views on the 'Jewish question.'

blocks.text_content: These early convictions were not formed in isolation. In Munich, Hitler found mentors and conspiratorial groups that refined his worldview.

Financed by wealthy industrialists, this group introduced him to the conspiracy theory linking international finance with Bolshevism. This blend of influences helped transform the DAP into something more recognizable.

Along with the name change, Hitler took charge of the party's visual identity, designing the iconic and menacing banner featuring a swastika in a white circle on a red background.

blocks.text_content: On February 24, 1920, the party released its **25-point programme**. Rather than a single, unified philosophy, this document was a collection of various ideas popular within the *volkisch* pan-Germanic movement, ranging from ultranationalism to a distrust of capitalism.

blocks.text_content: By 1921, Hitler had become a master of crowd manipulation, often speaking to thousands. However, not everyone was captivated. Some observers found his style erratic and aggressive, describing his speeches as more like preaching or bellowing than political discourse.

quote_block_data.speaker: Friedrich Reck-Malleczewen
quote_block_data.quote: He had come to a house where he had never been before, wearing gaiters, a floppy, wide-brimmed hat, and carrying a riding whip. ... Eventually, he managed to launch into a speech. He talked on and on, endlessly. He preached. He went on at us like a division chaplain in the Army. We did not in the least contradict him, or venture to differ in any way, but he began to bellow at us. The servants thought we were being attacked and rushed in to defend us. When he had gone, we sat silently, confused and not at all amused. There was a feeling of dismay, as when on a train you suddenly find you are sharing a compartment with a psychotic.
quote_block_data.context: In his 1947 book 'Diary of a Man in Despair', Reck-Malleczewen describes Hitler's erratic behavior and aggressive speech style during a visit.

blocks.text_content: Despite the mixed reactions, his ability to draw crowds made him indispensable to the party, a fact that became clear during a period of internal turmoil.

blocks.text_content: In June 1921, while Hitler was away in Berlin, a mutiny broke out in Munich. Executive committee members wanted to merge the Nazi Party with the **German Socialist Party (DSP)**. Hitler viewed this as a threat to his influence and responded with a calculated move: he resigned.

causal_chain_data.trigger: In June 1921, a mutiny broke out within the Nazi Party in Munich as executive committee members sought to merge with the German Socialist Party (DSP).
causal_chain_data.mechanism: Hitler resigned in protest on July 11, leading the committee to realize that losing their leading public figure and speaker would result in the end of the party.
causal_chain_data.outcome: On July 29, Hitler was granted absolute power as party chairman, succeeding Drexler, following a vote of 533 to 1.

blocks.text_content: The committee realized that without their star speaker, the party would collapse. Hitler used this leverage to demand absolute power as chairman, succeeding Drexler. By July 29, 1921, he was granted total control by a vote of 533 to 1.

blocks.text_content: By 1921, Hitler had become a master of crowd manipulation, often speaking to thousands. However, not everyone was captivated. Some observers found his style erratic and aggressive, describing his speeches as more like preaching or bellowing than political discourse.

quote_block_data.speaker: Friedrich Reck-Malleczewen
quote_block_data.quote: He had come to a house where he had never been before, wearing gaiters, a floppy, wide-brimmed hat, and carrying a riding whip. ... Eventually, he managed to launch into a speech. He talked on and on, endlessly. He preached. He went on at us like a division chaplain in the Army. We did not in the least contradict him, or venture to differ in any way, but he began to bellow at us. The servants thought we were being attacked and rushed in to defend us. When he had gone, we sat silently, confused and not at all amused. There was a feeling of dismay, as when on a train you suddenly find you are sharing a compartment with a psychotic.
quote_block_data.context: In his 1947 book 'Diary of a Man in Despair', Reck-Malleczewen describes Hitler's erratic behavior and aggressive speech style during a visit.

blocks.text_content: Despite the mixed reactions, his ability to draw crowds made him indispensable to the party, a fact that became clear during a period of internal turmoil.

blocks.text_content: In June 1921, while Hitler was away in Berlin on a fundraising trip, a mutiny broke out in Munich. Members of the party's executive committee sought to merge the Nazi Party with the Nuremberg-based German Socialist Party (DSP).

causal_chain_data.trigger: In June 1921, a mutiny broke out within the Nazi Party in Munich as executive committee members sought to merge with the German Socialist Party (DSP).
causal_chain_data.mechanism: Hitler resigned in protest on July 11, leading the committee to realize that losing their leading public figure and speaker would result in the end of the party.
causal_chain_data.outcome: On July 29, Hitler was granted absolute power as party chairman, succeeding Drexler, following a vote of 533 to 1.

blocks.text_content: With absolute power secured, Hitler began surrounding himself with loyalists like **Rudolf Hess**, **Hermann Goring**, and **Ernst Rohm**. To ensure the party could project force, he relied on a dedicated paramilitary arm.
